page: Vultr voc-c-2c-4gb-50s-amd is an entry-tier instance in the Optimized Cloud Compute family, engineered around an AMD EPYC processor on the x86_64 architecture. The server provides 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from a single physical core running 2 threads at 2.0 GHz, backed by 32 MB of L3 cache. It includes 4.0 GB of memory (2.0 GB per vCPU) and 50 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. Hardware acceleration is not present, as the configuration includes zero GPUs.

Benchmark evaluations reveal strong single-threaded processor throughput. The instance placed in the top tier of stress-ng single-core tests and achieved top-quartile results in Geekbench single-core execution, text processing, and single-threaded gzip and bzip3 operations. Conversely, total multi-threaded capability is constrained by the two-thread limit, resulting in lower-quartile placements in Clang compilation, ray tracing, and overall PassMark multi-core scores. Uncached memory read and write bandwidth remain in the middle tier, measuring 70.08 GB/sec and 63.38 GB/sec respectively.

By providing dedicated CPU allocation rather than shared or burstable cores, the voc-c-2c-4gb-50s-amd delivers predictable compute efficiency for applications that require consistent per-core execution. The primary trade-off centers on its constrained memory capacity and two-thread boundary, which cap concurrency. The instance is suited for lightweight microservices, small web APIs, background worker tasks, single-threaded batch processing, and low-traffic infrastructure management nodes.

The configuration includes 4.0 GB of RAM and 50 GB of local NVMe SSD storage, with no discrete GPU. Benchmark data shows strong single-threaded CPU capability, with top-tier stress-ng single-core execution alongside high ratings in single-threaded gzip compression and Geekbench text processing. However, multi-core throughput and parallelized tasks such as Clang compilation reflect the lower performance capacity inherent to a two-thread environment. Dedicated CPU resources ensure consistent latency without noisy-neighbor degradation common in shared platforms. This makes the instance cost-effective and operationally stable for lightweight microservices, low-concurrency web backends, CI build nodes with low parallelism, and text processing pipelines.
